"Charu, you asked why I always ask you where you feel it, not what you feel. Here is why.
When I was nine, my father moved us to Pune and I started a new school mid-year. Every morning at the gate I got a strange tight feeling in my belly and my legs went heavy. My mother asked, 'Reena, what is wrong?' I said, 'I feel funny.' That's all I had.
She took me to the doctor twice. Nothing was wrong with my stomach.
Then my aunt asked me a different question: 'Where does the funny feeling live?' I pointed at my belly. 'And what does it want?' I said, 'To go home.' She said, 'Maybe that's missing home, beti.' I cried, because it was true, and I hadn't known."

qa.a: She cried because it was true; she was relieved and moved to finally have words for the tight, funny feeling she had carried.

qa.q: What turning point in Reena's story helped her understand her feeling?
qa.a: Her aunt asking where the feeling lived and what it wanted, instead of what was wrong, helped Reena connect the belly ache to missing home.

qa.q: How might Reena's mother have felt taking her to the doctor twice?
qa.a: She was probably worried and puzzled, sensing something was wrong but not able to find it in Reena's stomach.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood feeling she could only call funny and point to in her belly, until someone helped her name it.

The school bus had broken down and the children were waiting on the hot pavement, forty minutes late already. Harsha, ten, sat on his bag, rubbing his chest.
"Are you sick?" his friend Divyansh asked.
"No. I feel... weird. Like here is tight." He pressed his chest. "And my hands are buzzing."
"Hungry?"
"No."
"Scared?"
Harsha frowned. "I don't know. Maybe? It's just weird."
The bus teacher heard and came over. "Harsha, you've got your maths test first period, haven't you?"
He nodded, slowly. "And we're late."
"So your body is worrying before you are," the teacher said. "Breathe with me. We'll tell your teacher you were delayed."
Harsha breathed. The tightness stayed a little, but it felt less strange once it had a reason.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling on the pavement, though he couldn't name it?
qa.a: He was anxious about his maths test and being late; his chest felt tight and his hands buzzed, but he could only call it weird.

qa.a: Divyansh guesses sick, hungry and scared, trying to help his friend find a word for what is going on.

Since the family's tomato crop failed in the hailstorm, Yogesh had gone quiet. His sister Alka noticed it at the bus stop in their village every morning.
"What's wrong?"
"Nothing."
"You didn't eat."
"Stomach hurts." It had hurt for a week. So had his back. He told the school nurse his head ached. He told his mother he was fine.
Alka tried again on the walk home. "Are you angry about the crop? Sad? Scared about fees?"
Yogesh kicked a stone. "I don't know. I'm just... fine. My body is tired." He wasn't cold to her; he walked closer to her than usual, and he waited when she stopped to buy peanuts. He just had no words for whatever sat in his chest.
That night Alka told their mother about the week of stomach aches.

Lucia's parents had been fighting since the spring. At dinner in their flat in Valencia, her uncle Siddiq, visiting from Manchester, asked, "How's school, how are you feeling about everything?"
"Fine."
"Just fine?"
"Yeah. Nothing's wrong." She pushed rice around the plate. "My neck's a bit stiff."

"And headache. I'm always tired."
"Lucia, if you had a word for what's in there, what would it be?"
She shrugged, not rudely. She leaned against him the way she had when she was small. "I don't know. I really don't. It's just heavy."
"Heavy is a good word to start with," he said, and stayed.

In the girls' hostel of the Pune junior college, the warden, Jyoti Ma'am, had seen Lavanya at the medical room three times that month.
"Headache again?"
"Yes, Ma'am. And stomach."
"Anything bothering you? Studies? Home?"
"No, Ma'am. I'm fine. Nothing."

Jyoti Ma'am pulled out a chart with feeling words and pictures. "Just point, if anything's close."
Lavanya looked for a long time. Her finger drifted to "homesick", then to "worried". "Maybe both? I don't know. I don't know how to say it."

Last year my manager called me "unreadable" in my appraisal. My friend Ujjwal said I answered every question with "it's okay". I, Tanvir, honestly didn't know what else to say. Inside there was only a kind of noise.
In March I went to a counsellor because I'd been snapping at my team and couldn't sleep. She didn't push. She gave me a wheel of feeling words and asked me to notice where things landed in my body.
So now I keep a small notebook. Tight jaw usually means frustrated. Hot neck means embarrassed. A hollow stomach, I'm learning, is lonely.
It is slow. Some days I write only "bad". But last week I told Ujjwal, "I felt left out when you didn't invite me," and he apologised. That sentence took me a year.

qa.a: The manager called Tanvir "unreadable".

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel about finally telling Ujjwal about being left out?
qa.a: Tanvir feels proud and a little amazed, since that sentence took a year of practice to be able to say.

qa.q: What would you advise someone starting this kind of practice, based on Tanvir's story?
qa.a: Start small with a notebook, link body cues like a tight jaw to words, accept days of only writing 'bad', and get a counsellor's help if it affects work or relationships.

Client: Zeenat, 24. Came in after her fiance Nilesh said she "never tells him anything" and her team lead flagged conflict at work. She described her feelings as "normal" or "off", and only physical: tight chest, heavy arms.
We have used a feeling-word list and a body map. She now writes three short lines each evening.
This week she arrived with her notebook open. "Tuesday: chest tight in meeting. Word: humiliated. Wednesday: arms heavy after Nilesh's call. Word: disappointed. Also relieved?" She laughed at having two words for one moment.
She says Nilesh now asks, "What's the word today?" and she can answer more often than not. We will continue fortnightly.

qa.a: The feeling-word list, the body map and the daily notes, which help Zeenat move from 'off' and a tight chest to words like humiliated and disappointed.
